newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian sugar -- Weak China buying caps Thai premiums.
newsitem.headline: Asian sugar -- Weak China buying caps Thai premiums.

text.p: Weaker Chinese buying is putting a lid on Thai sugar premiums despite a jump in demand from other parts of Asia, traders in Tokyo say.
They added regional demand was likely to remain tight until the end of the year.

Thai raw sugar premiums for January-March 1997 delivery are being quoted at up to 1.2 cents over New York March futures contracts, on a free on board (FOB) basis, down from 1.7 cents in early July, they said.
"Thai premiums continued to rise earlier this year as Thai raw sugar was almost sold out. Countries such as the Philippines and Indonesia were active buyers," a Tokyo-based sugar trader said.
Sugar consumption -- which tends to rise with growing disposable incomes -- is soaring in Asia on the back of a boom in soft drinks and sugary snacks such as ice cream.
"But the sharp drop in Chinese sugar buying this year was partly behind the gradual fall in Thai raw premiums," the trader said.
China's sugar imports in the first seven months of this year slumped by 52.6 percent to 760,000 tonnes compared with the year-ago period, Chinese custom figures showed.
Japan imported 860,705 tonnes of raw sugar in the first seven months of this year, against 874,783 tonnes in the same period a year earlier, Finance Ministry data showed.
Of that, 18,473 tonnes were imported in July from South Africa, which is recovering after a five-year-long drought which cut sugar exports sharply.
South African output for 1995/96 (October/September) was estimated at 2.4 million tonnes, of which about one million tonnes was expected to be exported.
"Sugar shipments from South Africa and Australia are taking place on schedule. Asian supply/demand is unlikely to tighten further," another Japanese sugar trader said.
The traders also said they were concerned about a new U.S. law aimed at restricting trade and investment with Cuba.

The Helms-Burton law, signed by President Bill Clinton in March, allows foreign concerns to be prosecuted in U.S. courts if they have "trafficked" in U.S. property seized in the 1959 Cuban revolution.

"We were told that some companies in Europe and Canada received warning letters from the U.S. government. But as far as we know, no Japanese trade houses have received such letters so far," a Trade Ministry official said.
Japan imported 92,111 tonnes of sugar from Cuba in the first seven months of this year, against 145,646 tonnes a year earlier, Finance Ministry data showed.
"Cuban sugar is increasingly becoming a sensitive issue politically," a trade house official said. "We're doing a lot of business in the U.S. and want to avoid unnecessary risk."
The traders said Cuba was expected to boost sugar shipments, particularly to China, as European traders were hesitant to handle Cuban sugar.
